Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
32-y/o with 2–3 day history of wheeze and exertional dyspnea; likely asthma exacerbation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: New wheeze and shortness of breath for 2–3 days.  
• Associated symptoms: Daytime cough without sputum or hemoptysis, subjective fever (self-checked temp 37 °C), occasional difficulty finishing sentences, limited exercise tolerance. No chest pain, no nocturnal symptoms.  
• Past asthma: Childhood asthma “quite bad,” required inhalers and occasional ED visits (no ICU). Salbutamol inhaler still used every few weeks and before exercise. Last formal asthma treatment stopped ~3–4 y ago.  
• Other atopy: Hay fever, eczema.  
• Medications: Salbutamol inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented. No other regular meds.  
• Allergies: None known.  
• Social: Non-smoker; drinks ~1 glass wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner. Engineer; currently working from home/sick leave due to symptoms. Preventive care not discussed.

Examination:
• Vitals: Self-reported temperature 37 °C.  
• No in-consult physical examination recorded.

Impression:
Likely acute asthma flare (possible viral or allergic trigger).

Plan:
• Continue salbutamol; increase to 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4 hrs as needed.  
• Prescribe spacer and peak-flow meter; pharmacist to demonstrate use.  
• Self-monitor peak flow twice daily (AM/PM) for 1 week; record values.  
• Start regular oral antihistamine (OTC) for hay fever; medication name per pharmacist.  
• Safety net: If fever develops or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens, contact service immediately.  
• Follow-up: Telephone/clinic review in 1 week with peak-flow diary; consider additional asthma controller therapy based on results.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Objective vitals (HR, BP, RR, SpO₂); medication doses; full allergy/meds reconciliation; vaccination status.  
● Internal conflicts: Patient stated asthma meds stopped 3–4 y ago yet also “normally” uses salbutamol every few weeks—conflict noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; occasional minor repetitions but clinically adequate.
